description: Right now we are the team of 2 students from the SJSU majoring in the Data Science and CS. We want to build the game that will be simulate real space missions that can be used to train future astronauts, but at the same time not be boring. Both of have the experience of developing the real world projects like: CV traction of missiles, AI training, ML models, hardware integration. We open to anyone who lives in Bay Area:)
summary:
Launch Window is a browser game where a crew of up to four (Mission Lead, Science Lead, Spacecraft Engineer, Comms & Ops) designs, launches and flies a space mission to spot wildfires or hunt for ice on the Moon. Every part trades off mass, power, money and data. Design reviews make your estimates grow, just like on real missions. You do the flight math yourself, and your thrust-to-weight and burn-time answers decide which orbit you reach. Then three years of operations bring solar storms, failures and budget cuts.

The final judge is real data. Your design is tested against real California wildfires from NIFC fire records, with live NASA FIRMS detections, above a NASA Blue Marble Earth. One rule decides everything: you only score for science that reaches the ground.

Play solo or scan a QR code to join your crew. There are three difficulty levels, and every number cites its source.

AI Used for video editing and voice

Project Details (paste this)

Launch Window is a browser game where players design, launch and fly a science mission, either solo or as a team of up to four on their own phones and laptops. It follows the real mission lifecycle: brief, roles, design, review, launch, operations, report and redesign.

How it works. Players pick a mission (Wildfire Watch over California, or Lunar Ice Hunter) and a difficulty level (Cadet, Engineer or Flight Director). Each player takes a role: Mission Lead, Science Lead, Spacecraft Engineer or Comms & Ops. Together they build a spacecraft from real classes of parts, including instruments, orbits, rockets, solar arrays, batteries, pointing systems, antennas, ground networks and data recorders. Every choice changes mass, power, cost and data, and the result appears live in a 3D hangar over NASA’s Blue Marble Earth. A design review grows the estimates, as happens on real missions, so margins matter. Players then do simple flight physics themselves (thrust-to-weight ratio and burn time), and their answers decide which orbit they reach. After launch, three years of operations play out in a few minutes, with solar storms, failures and budget cuts that the team votes on. The core rule is that a mission only scores for science that reaches the ground. An instrument that can’t be powered or can’t send its data down earns nothing. The mission report explains why, and the team redesigns.

Real data. The wildfire mission replays 8 real California fires from NIFC incident records, including the 2021 Dixie Fire, against the player’s design. Revisit time, pixel size and downlink delay decide how quickly the satellite would have alerted fire crews. Live NASA FIRMS detections show the fires burning today. Every part and number cites a public source, such as Landsat 9, MODIS, LRO, the Deep Space Network and NASA’s Small Spacecraft Technology State of the Art report.

Impact. The game teaches systems-engineering trade-offs, teamwork and basic physics to students and the public. It also shows why spacecraft design choices matter during real disasters. It runs in any browser with nothing to install, and teammates join by scanning a QR code.

Tools. TypeScript, React, Vite, Three.js and React Three Fiber for 3D, Vercel Functions and Upstash Redis for team rooms, and NASA FIRMS, NASA Scientific Visualization Studio and NIFC data. An AI coding assistant (Claude Code) helped write the code. The demo narration was generated with ElevenLabs.

Creativity and design choices. The demo opens with the story of a real fire, every player has a role, and real wildfires act as the final judge of each design. We kept the science honest by citing sources and keeping the physics simplified but correct. For accessibility there are solo play with in-game advisors, three difficulty levels and a 2D graphics option. Game balance was tuned with simulation scripts.
